The Big Story 

A link between Iran war and 9/11 in Trump administration speeches

President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth tied the Iran war to the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in remarks at the Pentagon, suggesting the conflict is a continuation of the war on terror.

AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein

“We salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said to claps from the audience at the ceremony.

 

Hegseth, speaking ahead of the president, said the U.S. remains “vigilant.”

 

“Our warriors have fought an Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century, that cheered on 9/11,” he said. 

 

“We’re still sending terrorists where they belong — to hell — and tankers to the bottom of the ocean, where they belong,” Hegseth added. “And we are ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

 

He reiterated that the U.S. controls the Strait of Hormuz and has destroyed Iran’s navy.

 

The global “war on terror” was declared shortly after the attacks in New York and lasted nearly 20 years, focusing on al Qaeda militants. The U.S. military withdrew from Afghanistan in August 2021.

 

Trump said earlier this week he sees the Iran war, which has already passed its six-month mark, lasting until the November midterm elections.

 

He said he thinks the war will “end immediately” after the election.

 

“They can’t hold out any longer,” Trump told reporters of Iran. “They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice, weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon.”

 

However, a Wall Street Journal report from Thursday said that Iran has resumed production of ballistic missiles, contradicting Trump administration claims that the country’s military capabilities have been destroyed.

 

Read the full report at thehill.com.

data.title: US Mint commemorating 9/11 with new half-dollar coin
data.description:
The U.S. Mint presented nearly 3,000 specially marked half dollar coins to the National September 11 Memorial & Museum on Friday to honor the victims of the 2001 and 1993 World Trade Center attacks.

The Enduring Liberty Half Dollar coins feature a special 9/11 privy mark on the front of the coin that reads “9-11-01” and “ALWAYS REMEMBER.”

The 2,983 coins represent the number of people killed on Sept. 11, 2001, and on Feb. 26, 1993, during the World Trade Center bombing. 

The coins were made at the Mint’s West Point facility in New York and delivered as the country marks 25 years since the 9/11 attacks on U.S. soil.

“This coin is a tangible representation of the strength it took for our nation to look forward, both 250 years ago at its founding, but more poignantly 25 years ago, as the world was changed forever,” Mint Director Paul Hollis said in a statement.

The front of the coin shows a close-up of the Statue of Liberty looking outward, along with the inscriptions “UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,” “IN GOD WE TRUST” AND “1776 ~ 2026.”

The back of the coin depicts Liberty passing her torch to a new generation that includes the phrase, “KNOWLEDGE IS THE ONLY GUARDIAN OF TRUE LIBERTY.”

A standard version of the Enduring Liberty Half Dollar, without the 9/11 privy mark, entered circulation at the beginning of 2026. It is being produced for one year only at the Mint’s Denver and Philadelphia facilities, according to the Mint.

The coin was authorized under a 2020 law that established new coin designs to commemorate the nation’s 250th anniversary. A coin with President Trump’s likeness was greenlit earlier this year as part of the celebrations, despite pushback stemming from a federal law prohibiting living people from being depicted on U.S. currency.

The Mint last week launched its $1 Trump coin, releasing 250,000 coins featuring a portrait of the president.

data.title: Proxy fight in Yemen heats up, risking new front in US-Iran war
data.description:
The Iranian-backed Houthi rebel group’s reported takeover of a Yemen port city is raising the stakes in Tehran’s war with the U.S.

Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s military, is reportedly urging President Trump to strike the rebels, while the U.S. has sent more than 100 advisors to aid its Saudi allies in the fight.

In a further escalation, Saudi Arabia on Friday said that it shut down the East-West Pipeline in the Riyadh and Madinah regions, later confirming the pipeline was attacked by “several” drones launched from Iraq, causing a “number of injuries.”

The pipeline, through which the kingdom can transfer 7 million barrels of crude, allows the country to transfer oil to the Red Sea after Iran effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz.

The Houthi’s Thursday takeover of Mokha, a port city vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea, gives Iran another possible foothold in the Middle East, as it can use the position to increase attacks or close the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a vital shipping lane for energy exports.

That point of leverage could further damage global energy markets already hampered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, according to analysts. 

Brett Erickson, a managing principal of Obsidian Risk Advisors, said that if the Houthis moved forward to a complete shutdown of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, it would be “checkmate” for the U.S. and global energy markets. 

“You’re losing millions of barrels per day. Yes, they can reroute with Suez [Canal]. You’re talking about weeks of essentially no flows due to the extra timeline. So it very much does become a checkmate at a time when Brent’s trading at $105, WTI is at $100, diesels at $6 a gallon,” Erickson said in a phone interview with The Hill on Friday, referring to the per-barrel costs of oil.

“It would just cut us out of runway,” he added.  

Mokha, about 50 miles from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, is of particular importance to controlling the waterway, through which about 12 percent of global goods flow.

Houthi forces also reportedly captured the island of Perim, which sits in the middle of the strait, according to multiple outlets. 

The takeovers come after the group in August renewed their attacks on Mokha, and its seizure would represent the biggest territorial gain for the Houthis since the group in 2022 signed an agreement to end a civil war that began in 2014.

Yemeni Air Force jets were bombing Houthis near Mokha on Friday, according to the government’s spokesperson. 

Since the start of the conflict between Washington and Tehran, the Houthis have increased attacks against Yemen’s government and declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia, which entered the war on the side of the internationally recognized government.

In early August, Houthi rebels fired missiles and drones at Saudi military targets in the eastern city of Marib, Yemen, where two people were killed and more than a dozen injured. 

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman has pressed Trump to take military action against the Houthis, with the two discussing the group’s developments at least twice in the 24 hours leading up to Friday morning, Axios reported. 

While Trump has so far declined to strike the Houthis, he has agreed to help the Saudis by  sharing military information and sending advisors to aid in developing targets on the group, two sources told the outlet.

Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed on Friday that maritime navigation is safe for all shipping companies besides Saudi Arabian ships, warning that the Houthi rebels could militarily escalate against Saudi-backed forces until the blockade on Yemen is lifted. 

The strikes on the crucial Saudi oil pipeline mark another major setback for Prince Mohammad.

The oil pumping station located near the town of Al Mesba’ah, Saudi Arabia, sustained extensive damage following the attack, a Friday Planet Labs satellite image, which was shared with The Hill, shows. 

Another pumping station near Al Dhekra, Saudi Arabia, was damaged in the attack, with dark smoke coming up, according to another image captured on Friday. 

Erickson said the shutdown of the pipeline by itself is not a “huge deal” on energy markets, as the Saudis can repair it, but the shutdown is not happening “in isolation.” 

“It’s in tandem with the Bab el-Mandeb, the Strait of Hormuz and 2 billion barrels of oil already lost and escalating tension in the region,” Erickson said. 

“So, in isolation, maybe survivable, obviously, but it’s in the more complete picture that becomes really concerning and it also just shows they can repair it. Sure, it can be hit again and again and again,” he added. “We just don’t have a solution to protect critical energy infrastructure.”

The developments come oil prices rose above $100 a barrel this week, the first time that figure has been hit since mid-May. 

Sabrina Singh, former Pentagon deputy press secretary, said the Houthis’ advance in recent days risks spilling over the Iran war into the region and could further imperil the global economy. 

“And we know that Saudi Arabia has had to, in fact, reroute a lot of the oil that it would get out through the strait — it was using the Red Sea and trying to even export it up through the Suez Canal,” Singh said during her Friday appearance on CNN. 

“With the Houthis now taking control of some of these two critical places, I think shipping is going to be further threatened, which means the global economy is going to be further upended.”

data.title: The debate over AI 'doomsday' warnings
data.description:
{beacon}

Technology

Technology

 

The Big Story 

Debate explodes over AI ‘doomsday’ warnings 

A former Anthropic researcher’s warning that AI could soon destroy humanity broke past the typical tech circles last week, setting off a new firestorm of debate over the technology’s rapid development. 

© Envato

Researchers have warned of AI’s potential danger for years, but nothing struck a chord quite like this week’s X thread from 27-year-old Jacob Coxon, a little-known AI researcher who resigned from Anthropic last week. 

 

Coxon, who worked at OpenAI and Anthropic, claimed in a post online that researchers at the firms “believe AI could kill all humans” but still push forward in a race to develop superintelligence — a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all humans’ cognitive performance. 

 

Coxon’s assessment went viral with over 165 million views and within a few hours, the debate over AI’s long-term implications was no longer confined within the technology community. 

 

Amid the media frenzy, many tech outsiders were left wondering exactly how AI could destroy humanity. The answer is not fully known, though researchers like Coxon say AI’s pace of development offers hints. 

 

Connor Leahy, an AI researcher leading the non-profit ControlAI that argues for ending development of superintelligence, said in an interview with The Hill he believes these agents will be entirely autonomous and “pursue their own objectives,” without human beings in mind. 

 

“There won’t just be one superintelligence,” Leahy told The Hill Thursday. “There will be millions of them running around, competing with each other, competing with humanity for resources, power, influence.” 

 

While Coxon’s warnings reached unlikely audiences, the underlying debate is nothing new for the tech sector. It is also no closer to a resolution. 

 

Read more in a full report Sunday at TheHill.com

data.title: CDC declares cyclospora outbreak over
data.description:
Click in for more news from The Hill
{beacon}

Healthcare

Healthcare

 

The Big Story 

CDC declares cyclospora outbreak over 

After nearly 13,000 cases and more than 500 hospitalizations, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said there is no longer any risk of contracting cyclosporiasis from the source linked to the outbreak. 

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

“At this time, there is no risk of people getting sick with cyclosporiasis from this source,” CDC wrote in the agency’s final update on the outbreak.  

 

Since cases began picking up in June, 21 states reported cyclosporiasis cases and two people with underlying health conditions died in Michigan. 

 

The lettuce, supplied by Taylor Farms in Mexico, is no longer available in stores or restaurants.  

 

The CDC is still investigating several case clusters of the parasitic illness nationwide. Including the multistate outbreak, CDC has received reports of 19,595 laboratory-confirmed cases of cyclosporiasis acquired in the United States.  

 

The FDA said it is continuing its investigation into the outbreak, including how the product became contaminated with cyclospora. Last month, the agency sent inspectors to the Taylor Farms processing center and lettuce farms in northeastern Mexico.  

 

Critics of the Trump administration cited the cyclosporiasis as another public health failure by the current Trump administration due to the CDC having scaled back its foodborne illness surveillance program last year, making monitoring for cyclospora voluntary instead of mandatory. 

 

Others noted, however, that the 10 states that were no longer required to report on cyclospora were not places the parasite hit hardest. 

 

In a letter to industry leaders, FDA’s acting deputy commissioner for food, Donald Prater, urged companies to invest more in cyclospora prevention and to follow food safety regulations.

data.title: Husted ousts his political director over posts with Nazi imagery
data.description:
Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) fired his campaign’s political director, Stephen Woytek, on Friday after learning about social media posts linked to Woytek, including a Facebook profile photo of Nazi officers and a public playlist of songs celebrating Rhodesia, a now-defunct nation often venerated by white supremacists. 

A spokeswoman for Husted’s campaign told The Hill that Woytek, who joined the campaign in August, had “denied negative intent” but said the senator had quickly opted to fire him after learning of the posts Friday.

“Steve serves our country honorably as a lieutenant in the U.S. Army and is a proud graduate of The Citadel. He studies military history and routinely reenacts historical battles. While he denies negative intent, his social media activity displays a complete lack of judgement and disregard for its impact on others,” the spokeswoman said. “Sen. Husted demands better of those who represent him. Upon learning about the social media posts today, Sen. Husted made the immediate decision to part ways.”

Woytek’s social media history included links to a military reenactment group whose members dress up as Nazi officers. There are public photos of Woytek in that attire with the group from 2018, when he would have been 16 years old, according to Washington Post, which was the first to report on Woytek’s posts and departure.

An account bearing his name also created a playlist on Spotify recently of songs celebrating Rhodesia, a former British colony in Africa where a white minority ruled over the African population. Some white supremacists have praised Rhodesia and expressed affinity with it, the Post reported.

Woytek, in a statement to the Post, said he should have “exercised better judgment when posting about my activities online” and did not want to distract from Husted’s race.

“I want to be unequivocal: I reject the racist and antisemitic ideology the SS and Nazi Germany represented. I believe it is important to educate our younger generations, which is why I participate in historical reenactments,” he said.

Husted, who is locked in a tight race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), is the second Republican candidate for Senate in recent months to let go of a staffer over their social media history. Rep. Mike Collins (R-Georgia) replaced his chief of staff Kip Talley in July, following reporting by Slate that Talley had been in a group chat with white supremacists and antisemites Nick Fuentes and Richard Spencer. 

Another former staffer for Collins had images on his own social media of a swastika and himself in Ku Klux Klan robes, according to the Post.

data.title: CIA releases never-before-seen warnings to Bush, Clinton about Al Qaeda
data.description:
The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) on Friday publicly released for the first time a tranche of daily intelligence briefings provided ahead of September 11, 2001 to former Presidents George W. Bush and Bill Clinton about Al Qaeda’s plans to commit terrorist attacks on U.S. soil.

The intelligence agency released 71 declassified documents in what CIA Director John Ratcliffe called “an act of exceptional transparency” on the 25th anniversary of this tragic day. This is the single-largest release ever of the agency’s analysis of this terrorist attack, according to Ratcliffe.

“25 years ago, the 9/11 attacks struck a blow to our Nation, but they did not break us,” Ratcliffe said in a statement. “Generations of CIA officers have since dedicated their careers to securing justice for our fallen Americans and ensuring al-Qa’ida would never again harm our country.”

“In the years that followed, numerous CIA officers made the ultimate sacrifice in the Global War on Terror,” the CIA director continued. “We honor their memory and service through our commitment to disrupt, dismantle, and defeat those who wish to cause us harm.”

The files include a warning that Clinton received from the agency during his presidency in 1998. The memo, dated Sept. 10 of that year, warned that Al Qaeda “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a U.S. city.”

The 9/11 Commission noted this memo in its 2004 study but did not mention that it was included in the then-president’s daily briefing. Items in the commander in chief’s daily briefings are among the most sensitive documents and only shared with the president and a small circle of national security advisers.

While these newly-declassified CIA documents do not appear to contain major revelations about these attacks, they do provide a window into the information these two commanders-in-chief received in the lead up to this tragic day. 

Earlier on Friday, a 9/11 victim’s widow, Terry Strada, called on the Trump administration to hold Saudi Arabia accountable for these attacks during a remembrance ceremony in New York City. 

Strada accused former presidents present at this event of withholding evidence and choosing to “protect the Saudis instead of standing with the 9/11 families.”

“They broke promises, both public and private,” she said. “It has been one betrayal after another.”

Fifteen of Al Qaeda’s plane hijackers were Saudi nationals, and Strada and other family members of 9/11 victims believe the Saudis were complicit in these attacks — an accusation the kingdom has repeatedly denied. 

The widow called on President Trump to “tell the Saudis to stop lying.”

“Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through,” Strada said. 

The Hill has reached out to the White House regarding Strada’s request.

data.title: Stubborn inflation raises prospect of Fed rate hike
data.description:
The Federal Reserve appears increasingly likely to hike interest rates next week, as inflation remains stubbornly elevated amid the war with Iran. 

New data out Friday showed annual inflation remained unchanged in August, still well above the central bank’s target 2 percent rate. This is raising expectations of a rate hike, even as President Trump pushes for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh to cut rates.

“There’s no guarantee that the Fed will hike next week, but it’s hard to see how the central bank can justify leaving rates on hold,” Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management, said in a statement after the consumer price index (CPI) data was released Friday.

Jai Kedia, a research fellow at the Center for Monetary and Financial Alternatives at the libertarian think tank Cato Institute, said he has been advocating for the Fed to raise rates all year but suggested the central bank has lagged behind the realities of the economy. 

“This is a standard problem now with the Fed and the way it’s been doing policy over the past five or six years is that they tend to respond to economic developments way too slowly, and by the time they do so, the economic scenario has changed,” he said. 

“I think that it’s probably fine for them to raise interest rates by 25 basis points,” he continued. “But the macroeconomic realities were much worse the whole year when they chose not to raise.” 

The central bank’s rate-setting panel is poised to meet Tuesday and Wednesday, with investors pricing in a nearly 87 percent chance that it hikes rates by a quarter-point, according to the CME FedWatch tool. 

The CPI, a popular measure of inflation, rose 0.4 percent last month and 3.4 percent over the past 12 months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). 

While this was largely in line with expectations, core CPI, which excludes more volatile food and energy prices, came in slightly hotter than expected, ticking up 0.3 percent in August. 

“That was not what the Fed wanted to see,” Ryan Nunn, director of research for the Budget Lab, told The Hill. “It would like to see continued decline in inflation, and markets are responding to this by increasing their expectation of a rate hike next week.”

White House spokesperson Kush Desai argued the data “reinforces how President Trump’s targeted policy interventions are paying off, with dramatic month-over-month price reductions for beef, prescription drugs, and car insurance.”

“These policies are having a lasting effect for everyday Americans, and will continue delivering as energy supplies increase, markets stabilize, and overall inflation declines again,” he continued. 

Looking at overall inflation, one of the key drivers of the monthly uptick in prices was gas, BLS noted Friday. Gas prices rose 3.9 percent in August alone, accounting for more than a third of the increase last month.

Energy prices have surged amid the war with Iran. As the conflict has flared up once again in recent weeks, oil prices have jumped, with both the global and U.S. benchmarks crossing $100 a barrel Friday afternoon. 

The average price of diesel also hit a record Friday at $6.05 a gallon, up 63 percent from a year ago, according to AAA.  

This surge in energy prices “will probably tip the scale to a hike at next week’s meeting,” Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Commercial Bank, said in a statement. 

Meanwhile, signs of stability in the labor market are also raising pressure on the Fed to hike rates. The August jobs report came in stronger than expected last week, with U.S. employers adding 162,000 jobs. 

The central bank is tasked with a balancing act often referred to as its dual mandate, in which it aims for maximum employment and stable prices. If the labor market is in relatively solid shape, this shifts the focus to inflation.

“On the employment side of the Fed’s dual mandate, our country is doing well. Labor markets are quite stable,” Warsh said last month at a gathering of central bankers in Jackson Hole, Wyo., adding, “But on the price-stability side of our mandate, the numbers are more concerning.” 

He pointed to the personal consumer expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. It showed annual inflation staying flat at 3.7 percent in July.

“None of these measures are perfect, but they all tell a similar story: Inflation is running above our 2 percent target,” Warsh said. “So the Fed’s predominant focus right now should be on prices.” 

Lindsey Piegza, chief economist for Stifel Financial, suggested some Fed officials may be open to a “more patient approach” on rates. She noted that year-over-year core CPI sat at 2.4 percent, its lowest level in several years.

Friday’s data “reinforces the storyline of accelerating prices and underscores the need for firmer policy,” Piegza told The Hill.

“However, given the cooling in the core to a multiyear low, there is still a sizable portion of the committee that would support a more patient approach to policy adjustments and be willing, as [Fed Governor Chris] Waller said, to give disinflation a chance,” she added. 

Waller said earlier this month that “if there is continued progress toward our 2 percent goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level.” 

Kedia, however, argued that he thinks the best time to raise the rates would’ve been around March or April. 

As Warsh braces for next week’s meeting, he is also grappling with increasingly forceful demands from Trump to cut rates. This has long been a fixation for the president, who repeatedly feuded with Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, on the issue. 

Trump has given Warsh some breathing room at his first meetings leading the central bank, but it’s unclear how long this will last. After last week’s jobs report, the president called on the Fed to slash rates, threatening to halt trade with numerous countries if it does not. 

“The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change,” he wrote in a post on Truth Social. “High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen!” 

National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said in July that he saw “no excuse” for raising rates. 

Vance also chimed in last week, suggesting the Fed should lower interest rates to help ease mortgage rates. The 30-year mortgage rate hit a 14-month high on Thursday, climbing to 6.76 percent amid a rise in global bond yields. 

Despite this, some analysts now see even more rate hikes on the horizon. 

“We do not expect the Fed to be one-and-done,” Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said in a statement. 

“This is no longer simply about fine-tuning the economy,” she continued. “After half a decade of above-target inflation, policymakers are likely to conclude that more than one hike will be needed to re-establish price stability.” 

Shah suggested that October may be “politically challenging” for another hike given the nearness of the midterm elections, making the next meeting in December “the most likely opportunity for the Fed to deliver a follow-up hike.”

data.title: Contractor blames Lincoln Memorial problems on itself, not vandals: Report
data.description:
The contractor behind the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool renovation says mistakes made during the repair caused the pool’s new blue liner to peel and blister, according to a new report.

Atlantic Industrial Coatings found that workers did not apply enough primer in some areas and that two materials used for the liner were not compatible, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times.

The findings contrast claims of vandalism made by President Trump, who has repeatedly blamed vandals for the damage found at the pool despite the Justice Department dropping charges against several people accused of damaging the liner.

The company said one of the materials became too hot for the layer underneath it, causing parts of the liner to bubble and come loose, in an apparent worker oversight.

Atlantic is now repairing the pool, which remains drained while the work continues, under warranty.

The problems come months after the Trump administration gave Atlantic a $14.7 million no-bid contract to renovate the pool ahead of July 4 celebrations commemorating the nation’s 250th birthday.

But the pool’s renovation came with shortfalls after reports of peeling paint and damage to the liner became a source of controversy. Trump blamed the damage on vandals, accusing people of using knives or other sharp objects to cut the liner.

Federal prosecutors initially brought vandalism charges against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn and others accused of the damage, but the DOJ dismissed the cases in July after documents showed the problems occurred during installation.

Trump acknowledged that there had been some contractor error but maintained that vandalism also occurred.

Atlantic did find cuts to caulking around the edge of the pool that is attributed to vandalism, according to the Times. But the company did not link those cuts to the peeling liner covering the bottom of the pool.

data.title: TikTok misled consumers about filtering content for minors, judge rules
data.description:
A Texas judge on Thursday ruled the social media platform TikTok misled consumers about the company’s efforts to filter inappropriate content for minors.

In her ruling, Texas District Judge Cory Liu said TikTok’s claims about its content-moderation policies violated the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

The state of Texas alleged TikTok did not remove certain categories of videos, including sexually suggestive or graphic content or promotions of gambling or drugs, that violated the platform’s Community Guidelines.

The internal content-moderation policies, according the state, “instructed that such content should be allowed to remain on the platform with the designation of ‘hard to find’ rather than ‘do not allow,'” according to court filings.

The state also argued TikTok misled users when claiming its “Restricted Mode” effectively filtered out content potentially inappropriate for minors.

Prosecutors alleged TikTok employees internally acknowledged the restricted mode did not work as intended and “exposed users to a high amount of content that should have been filtered out,” the filing stated.

Liu ruled the state met the burden for summary judgement on both allegations, allowing the trial to move forward. The trial, which is expected to be set for next month, would mark the first full trial on safety claims for TikTok if a settlement is not reached beforehand.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) celebrated Liu’s ruling Thursday, writing TikTok “sacrificed the safety and innocence of children for engagement and numbers, and now they are being held accountable.”

TikTok did not respond to request for comment.

TikTok is among a handful of social media companies to face increasing pressure rover its ability to protect children online.

The trial will follow two landmark verdicts earlier this year that found the social media giant Meta liable for its platforms’ impact on kids and teen mental and physical health.

Last month, Meta settled a similar case with nearly every state in the U.S., agreeing to pay more than $17 billion and roll out several platform changes. Texas was not part of this settlement, but revealed hours later it reached a separate agreement with Meta, bringing the company’s total sum to just over $18 billion.

In announcing the settlement, Meta specifically called out YouTube and TikTok to “join” the company in adopting what it calls a “new standard” for kids online safety. 

In an open letter, Meta argued the benefits of its new standards will only be “truly effective” if other industry players follow the same standard, putting public pressure on its rivals to make a deal. 

TikTok has largely stayed quiet, providing no public response on the letter.
